newsitem.title: USA: CFTC chair concerned about some U.S. legal reforms.
newsitem.headline: CFTC chair concerned about some U.S. legal reforms.

text.p: The new chairwoman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said she has significant concerns about some portions of a Congressional proposal to amend U.S. commodities law.
Senators Richard Lugar and Patrick Leahy introduced a bill earlier this month that would make a dozen changes in the Commodity Exchange Act, the primary U.S. law governing futures trading.
"We are examining the provisions," Brooksley Born said in an interview with Reuters. "There are some that cause me some significant concern and others that don't."
In particular, Born raised concerns about a proposal intended to speed the approval process for new futures contracts.
Under the present law, the CFTC reviews all new contracts and generally grants approval for trading within a few months.

The Lugar-Leahy bill would create a legal presumption that new contracts should be approved and allow trading to begin in 10 business days unless the CFTC objects. If an objection is raised, the contract can trade in another 15 days unless the CFTC institutes proceedings to disapprove.

"One provision that does cause me concern, because I think it may be unworkable from a regulatory point of view, is the provison that amends the contract designation process," Born said. "It seems quite cumbersome and perhaps unworkable."
But Born said the CFTC is still evaluating the legislation and welcomed the opportunity to reassess current laws.

"I think it's important for regulatory agencies to review their governing statute periodically to make sure that it gives them the power that they need, that it stays up to date," said Born, an attorney at Arnold & Porter before being sworn in last month as the seventh chair of the CFTC.
The Senators, however, are unlikely to back down on the contract designation provision, a spokesman for the Agriculture Committee said on Friday.
"We have our bill and it is a well thought through position," spokesman Andy Fischer said reacting to Born's comment. "There's certainly not going to be any change in it."

The bill is not expected to pass this year, but will be revived in 1997. The bill and a measure in the House of Representatives proposed by Rep. Charles Schumer would give the CFTC additional power over foreign futures contracts that accept delivery in the United States.

The senate bill would grant additonal power to get information about delivery warehouses, while the Schumer bill would subject foreign contracts to U.S. rules in some cases. Most of Sumitomo Corp's trading was done on the London Metal Exchange but copper was kept at a U.S. warehouse.
Born signaled that the CFTC might ask for additional information gathering power.

"One point that is raised by both bills os whether we have sufficient information gathering powers from U.S. warehouses of foreign exchanges in a situation where we don't have an ongoing formal investigation," Born said.
In such cases, the CFTC lacks subponea power, Born noted. "That is an area we have been looking at and we'll try to determine whether we have sufficient regulatory powers."

Of allegations that the LME was not forthcoming with the CFTC last year, Born said she was not familiar with the "day to day requests" made of the LME. But by "late last year, we became very pleased with the amount of information sharing."
At that time, information from the LME was forwarded to the CFTC from United Kingdom securities regulators, she said. The CFTC is "pleased with the level of cooperation since then," she said.
